subject: business-studies
promptStrong: Give me a challenging GCSE exam-style question on AQA Business human resources (organisational structure, recruitment, training and motivation), then mark my answer against the spec.
promptWeak: Explain an AQA GCSE Business human resources idea for GCSE Business simply, with an example and the most common mistake.
learningObjectives: Organisational structures: hierarchy, span of control, chain of command, delayering and delegation
Tall vs flat structures and centralisation vs decentralisation
The need for recruitment and internal vs external recruitment

Contracts of employment and types of working arrangement
The importance of a motivated workforce
The importance and benefits of training

questions.lo: Organisational structures: hierarchy, span of control, chain of command, delayering and delegation
questions.q: In an organisational structure, what does 'span of control' mean?
options: The number of employees a manager is directly responsible for
The passing of authority down the hierarchy to subordinates
The number of layers of management in the business
The route a decision travels from the top to the bottom
questions.explain: Span of control is the number of subordinates a manager directly supervises. The layers of management is the levels of hierarchy, the route decisions travel is the chain of command, and passing authority down is delegation.

questions.lo: Organisational structures: hierarchy, span of control, chain of command, delayering and delegation
questions.q: A manager passes authority for a task down to a subordinate while keeping overall responsibility. What is this called?
options: Chain of command
Centralisation
Delegation
Delayering
questions.explain: Delegation is giving a subordinate the authority to carry out a task; the manager remains ultimately responsible. Delayering is removing management levels, chain of command is the line of authority, and centralisation keeps decisions at the top.

questions.lo: Tall vs flat structures and centralisation vs decentralisation
questions.q: A business removes two levels of middle management to create a flatter structure. What is the most likely immediate effect on the remaining managers?
options: Their span of control becomes wider
Delegation to staff becomes impossible
The chain of command becomes longer
Their span of control becomes narrower
questions.explain: Delayering into a flatter structure means each remaining manager supervises more people, so spans of control widen. The chain of command actually shortens, and flatter structures usually require MORE delegation, not less.

questions.lo: Tall vs flat structures and centralisation vs decentralisation
questions.q: Which statement best describes a decentralised business?
options: Decision-making authority is shared out to lower levels or local branches
All major decisions are made by senior managers at head office
The business has removed all middle managers
The business has a very tall organisational structure
questions.explain: Decentralisation delegates decision-making down to lower levels or local sites, which can speed up decisions and motivate staff. Keeping decisions with senior managers at head office is centralisation.

questions.lo: The need for recruitment and internal vs external recruitment
questions.q: Which of the following is a benefit of INTERNAL recruitment rather than external recruitment?
options: The candidate is already known to the business and it is cheaper and quicker
It usually attracts a larger pool of applicants
It avoids the need to train the successful candidate at all
It brings in fresh ideas and new skills from outside
questions.explain: Internal recruitment fills a post from existing staff, so the candidate is already known, and it is typically cheaper and faster. Bringing in fresh ideas and a larger applicant pool are advantages of external recruitment.

questions.lo: Stages and documents of recruitment and selection
questions.q: Which document lists the qualifications, skills and experience an ideal candidate should have?
options: Job description
Contract of employment
Job advertisement
Person specification
questions.explain: The person specification describes the ideal candidate (skills, qualifications, experience). The job description sets out the duties and responsibilities of the role itself, while the contract sets out terms of employment.

questions.lo: Stages and documents of recruitment and selection
questions.q: A firm carries out job analysis and then writes a document setting out the tasks, duties and responsibilities of the vacant role. Which document is this?
options: Payslip
Reference
Person specification
Job description
questions.explain: The job description outlines the duties and responsibilities of the post. A person specification instead describes the ideal person to fill it. Job analysis is the process that informs both.

questions.lo: Contracts of employment and types of working arrangement
options: A contract where the employer is not obliged to provide any minimum hours of work
A contract guaranteeing a fixed 40-hour week
A contract that automatically ends after zero months
A contract shared equally between two employees
questions.explain: Under a zero-hour contract the employer does not guarantee any minimum hours; the worker is only paid for hours actually worked. Two people splitting one full-time post is a job share.

questions.lo: Contracts of employment and types of working arrangement
questions.q: A cafe hires extra staff only on busy weekends and offers no guaranteed weekday hours. Which contract type best suits this need for flexibility?
options: Full-time permanent contract
Fixed 35-hour salaried contract
Zero-hour contract
Job share
questions.explain: A zero-hour contract lets the cafe call staff in only when demand is high, giving maximum flexibility and keeping wage costs down during quiet periods. A full-time or fixed-hours contract would commit the business to paying for hours it does not need.

questions.lo: The importance of a motivated workforce
questions.q: Which of these is a likely benefit to a business of having a well-motivated workforce?
options: More frequent absenteeism
Lower productivity
Improved staff retention and higher productivity
Higher labour turnover
questions.explain: A motivated workforce tends to be more productive and stays with the business longer (better retention), which reduces recruitment costs. Motivation lowers, not raises, labour turnover and absenteeism.

questions.q: A salesperson is paid an extra amount for every product they sell, on top of a basic wage. This financial method of motivation is called:
options: Fringe benefit
Commission
Profit sharing
Salary
questions.explain: Commission is a payment based on the number or value of sales made, directly rewarding output. A salary is a fixed annual amount, while profit sharing distributes a portion of company profits to staff.

questions.q: Which of the following is a FINANCIAL method of motivation?
options: Offering more training opportunities
Giving employees greater responsibility
Improving the style of management
Profit sharing among staff
questions.explain: Profit sharing gives staff a monetary reward, so it is a financial method. Greater responsibility, a better management style and training are non-financial methods of motivation.

questions.q: Which of the following is a NON-financial method of motivating staff?
options: Awarding an annual bonus
Introducing a commission scheme
Giving employees more responsibility and varied work
Paying a higher hourly wage
questions.explain: Giving greater responsibility and more varied work motivates without extra pay, so it is non-financial. Higher wages, bonuses and commission are all financial methods.

questions.q: A manager cannot afford pay rises but wants to lift morale. Which non-financial approach fits the AQA spec?
options: Cutting the number of holidays
Paying a one-off cash bonus
Increasing everyone's commission rate
Adopting a more supportive style of management and offering fringe benefits
questions.explain: Improving the style of management and offering fringe benefits (such as staff discounts or free parking) are non-financial motivators that raise morale without direct pay rises. Commission and cash bonuses are financial methods.

questions.lo: The importance and benefits of training
questions.q: Which of these is a benefit to a business of training its employees?
options: Higher labour turnover
Increased productivity and higher quality output
Lower productivity
Reduced ability to cope with new technology
questions.explain: Training raises productivity, quality and the ability to handle new technology, and it improves motivation and retention. It should reduce, not increase, labour turnover.

questions.lo: Methods of training: induction, on-the-job and off-the-job
questions.q: What is the main purpose of INDUCTION training?
options: To introduce a new employee to the business, their role and its procedures
To reward staff for meeting sales targets
To send staff on an external college course
To retrain long-serving staff on new machinery
questions.explain: Induction training helps a new employee settle in by explaining their role, colleagues, health and safety and workplace procedures. Retraining and external courses are separate forms of on-the-job or off-the-job training.

questions.lo: Methods of training: induction, on-the-job and off-the-job
questions.q: Which statement correctly describes OFF-the-job training?
options: Employees learn while carrying out their normal job at their workstation
Training is delivered only by a fellow team member on the shop floor
Training only takes place on an employee's first day
Employees are trained away from the workplace, for example at a college or training centre
questions.explain: Off-the-job training happens away from the normal work position, such as at a college or specialist training centre. Learning while doing the actual job at the workstation is on-the-job training.

questions.lo: Methods of training: induction, on-the-job and off-the-job
questions.q: A small garage wants to train a new mechanic cheaply while the business keeps running. Which method is usually the most cost-effective and keeps the mechanic productive?
options: No training at all
On-the-job training alongside an experienced mechanic
A one-year full-time college course
Sending the mechanic abroad for external training
questions.explain: On-the-job training lets the new mechanic learn from an experienced colleague while still doing useful work, so it is usually cheaper and keeps output going. A long external course is costly and removes the mechanic from the workplace.

questions.lo: The importance of a motivated workforce
questions.q: A firm suffers high labour turnover and low output. Which combination of measures best addresses BOTH motivation and retention per the AQA spec?
options: Remove all fringe benefits to save money
Cut wages and increase the span of control
Stop all induction training for new staff
Improve pay, offer training and give staff more responsibility
questions.explain: Combining a financial method (better pay) with non-financial methods (training and greater responsibility) tackles both motivation and retention, reducing turnover and raising productivity. Cutting pay or benefits would worsen the problem.
